title: Linux Networking Tools
description: Explore modern and classic networking utilities including ip, ss, netstat, curl, dig, and traceroute for connectivity diagnostics.

tasks.prompt: On Ubuntu, ip from iproute2 is installed. As an ordinary user, use ip to display the IPv4 and IPv6 addresses and link states of every interface in the current network namespace.
tasks.explanation: ip addr show lists addresses and interface state in the current network namespace. With no family or device filter it includes IPv4 and IPv6 on all interfaces; displaying this information needs no sudo. An administratively UP interface may still lack carrier or connectivity.

tasks.prompt: On Ubuntu, ip from iproute2 is installed and eth0 exists in the current network namespace. You are an ordinary user with sudo access and no network administration capability. Use sudo and ip to bring eth0 administratively UP.
aliases: sudo ip link set eth0 up
tasks.hint: Use sudo ip link set eth0 up.
tasks.explanation: sudo runs ip with the network administration privilege needed to change eth0. The up flag enables the interface administratively; it does not assign an address, configure a route, establish physical carrier, or guarantee connectivity. This changes runtime state, not persistent Ubuntu network configuration.

tasks.prompt: On Ubuntu, ip from iproute2 is installed. As an ordinary user, use ip to display all routes in the IPv4 main routing table of the current network namespace.
tasks.explanation: ip route show defaults to the IPv4 main table (table 254). Explicit -4 and table main select the same table. It needs no sudo and does not show every policy-routing table or the IPv6 routing table; ip route get instead resolves one destination.

tasks.prompt: On Ubuntu, ss from iproute2 is installed. You are an ordinary user with sudo access; TCP listeners in the current network namespace include processes owned by other users. Use sudo and ss to list only all TCP listening sockets (IPv4 and IPv6), with numeric addresses and ports and their owning process information. Assume root can inspect their /proc entries.
tasks.explanation: ss selects TCP (-t), listening sockets (-l), numeric addresses and ports (-n), and owning processes (-p). sudo allows inspection of other users' process file descriptors in /proc in this scenario. Process information can be unavailable if a process exits or access is restricted; a listener does not prove remote reachability. The equivalent state listening filter can replace -l.

tasks.prompt: On Ubuntu, netstat from net-tools is already installed. As an ordinary user, use netstat to list only all listening TCP sockets (IPv4 and IPv6) in the current network namespace, with numeric addresses and ports. Process information is not requested.
tasks.explanation: netstat -tln selects TCP (-t), listening sockets only (-l), and numeric addresses and ports (-n). This read-only listing needs no sudo. net-tools is an additional installed utility in this scenario; ss provides the modern replacement. Listening locally does not prove a firewall permits remote access.

tasks.prompt: On Ubuntu, curl is installed with default options, DNS and HTTPS access work, and https://example.com/ supports HEAD with a direct response and a trusted certificate. As an ordinary user, use curl to fetch only the HTTP response headers for that HTTPS root URL.
tasks.explanation: curl -I (or --head) sends HTTP HEAD and displays response headers without downloading the response body. HTTPS uses TLS and certificate verification. -i includes headers along with a GET body; -X HEAD alone changes the request method without putting curl into its proper HEAD handling mode.

tasks.prompt: On Ubuntu with Bash, curl is installed with default options and your current directory is /home/user, which you own and can write. app.tar.gz does not exist. Assume https://releases.example.com/app.tar.gz is an accessible scenario URL returning the archive directly over trusted HTTPS, with no redirect. Use curl to download its response body into /home/user/app.tar.gz.
tasks.explanation: curl -o (or --output) saves the response body to the named local file. -O uses the URL basename, app.tar.gz, so it also meets this scenario. Bash > redirects the body into that file. No sudo is needed in your writable directory. The command alone does not verify an archive checksum or authenticity beyond HTTPS certificate verification.

tasks.prompt: On Ubuntu, BIND dig is installed, its default IN-class options are unchanged (no .digrc overrides), and /etc/resolv.conf identifies a reachable DNS resolver. As an ordinary user, use dig to query MX records for example.com through the configured resolver.
tasks.explanation: dig queries DNS mail-exchanger (MX) records for example.com, using a resolver from /etc/resolv.conf when no @server is given. The -t option explicitly selects MX; a trailing dot makes the name absolute. An MX reply describes mail-routing preferences and hosts, not whether their SMTP service is reachable. This query needs no sudo.

tasks.prompt: On Ubuntu, BIND dig is installed with unchanged default IN-class options (no .digrc overrides), and /etc/resolv.conf identifies a reachable DNS resolver. As an ordinary user, use dig to query A records for google.com through that resolver and print a short answer rather than the verbose DNS report.
tasks.explanation: dig +short requests terse answer output; A is the default query type and can also be stated explicitly or selected with -t A. A records contain IPv4 addresses. A short answer may include CNAME targets as well as addresses, and an empty answer does not by itself explain a lookup failure. No sudo is needed.

tasks.prompt: On Ubuntu, traceroute from the traceroute package is installed and an IPv4 route to 8.8.8.8 is configured. As an ordinary user, use traceroute with its default UDP method (destination ports starting at 33434 and increasing per probe) to trace hops toward 8.8.8.8.
tasks.explanation: traceroute sends probes with increasing TTL and reports responding hops and round-trip times. The installed utility's default UDP method is allowed for unprivileged users. -n suppresses hostname lookups; -4 explicitly selects IPv4. A * means no response arrived before the timeout, not proof that a router is down; filtering or rate limiting can hide hops.

tasks.prompt: On Ubuntu, hostname is installed. The current short hostname is lab, and the system resolver maps lab to the canonical fully qualified name lab.example.com (for example through /etc/hosts). As an ordinary user, use hostname to display that resolver-derived FQDN.
tasks.explanation: hostname -f (also --fqdn or --long) resolves the current hostname and prints its canonical fully qualified name. The result depends on resolver configuration such as /etc/hosts or DNS; a machine may have no usable FQDN or multiple names. This read-only command needs no sudo and does not set the hostname.

tasks.prompt: On Ubuntu, iputils ping is installed, an IPv4 route to 1.1.1.1 exists, and your ordinary user account is allowed to create ICMP echo sockets. Use ping to send exactly three IPv4 ICMP echo requests to 1.1.1.1, without a deadline that could stop it early.
tasks.explanation: ping -c 3 stops after sending three ECHO_REQUEST packets; it does not require three replies. The numeric destination is IPv4, which -4 can state explicitly. sudo is unnecessary when ICMP echo sockets are allowed as assumed here. Echo replies test ICMP reachability, not whether a TCP service is available; packet loss can reflect filtering as well as network failure.
